edges.description: Parenchymal cysts are initially tolerated, then degenerate under a host inflammatory reaction that arises either by natural evolution or after antiparasitic treatment.
edges.source: Larval infection of the nervous system (neurocysticercosis)

edges.description: Cysts lodged in the ventricles and subarachnoid cisterns follow a different course from parenchymal cysts, remaining hidden from immune surveillance for years.
edges.source: Larval infection of the nervous system (neurocysticercosis)
edges.target: Extraparenchymal Cyst Burden with Impaired CSF Flow

edges.description: Degenerating cysts are walled off in a granuloma that finally calcifies, leaving residual calcifications rather than resolving completely.
The calcified granulomas are what appears as hyperdense lesions on brain CT.
Calcified lesions act as chronic seizure foci; human biopsy shows perilesional gliosis, oedema and blood-brain barrier disruption at these sites.
Calcified NCC has been associated with headache, proposed to follow remodeling of the calcification and release of antigen remnants into the parenchyma.
Impaired CSF flow accumulates CSF in the ventricles.

nodes.description: Antiparasitic drugs are used to kill brain parasites in neurocysticercosis.

nodes.description: In the ventricles and subarachnoid cisterns, two mechanisms impair CSF flow: inflammation once the immune system recognizes cyst antigens (arachnoiditis, basal fibrosis, ependymitis), and direct mechanical obstruction by the cysts themselves, which can cause hydrocephalus even without inflammation.
